To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genetic background of cancer predisposition and progression is very complex and multifactorial, the identification of low/moderate cancer risk markers is a long and tedious process that will take many years and that testing for such markers in routine diagnostics is not feasible at present.

the identification of low/moderate cancer genetic risk markers is of high scientific relevance, that the use of the data in routine medical practice is premature, but that the data might have a role in individualized cancer prevention, surveillance, or treatment in the near future.

the genetic background of cancer is complex and multifactorial, that the identification of low/moderate risk genetic markers is a very difficult task, that there is still no clear evidence for the benefit of testing for such markers in routine practice, that the use of genetic information for the prediction of disease risk in general is still in its early stages and that there is still a long way to go before we can apply this knowledge in routine diagnostics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular and genetic background of complex diseases, including cancer, in order to identify new therapeutic targets and develop novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
the identification of genetic markers that may predict the development of a disease in the future.
the development of novel approaches in the field of molecular medicine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of genetic markers in cancer risk prediction should be restricted to those cases in which there is a clear evidence for the causality of a specific genetic alteration in cancer development.
the use of low/moderate risk genetic markers in medical practice is still premature and should not be recommended at this time.
testing for genetic markers of low/moderate genetic predisposition for cancer is not yet recommended for use in routine medical practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current state of the art in genetic risk prediction for complex diseases is not yet mature enough to be used in routine diagnostics.
we have to learn more about the genetic basis of multifactorial diseases before we can use the data for clinical purposes.
the identification of genetic variants with moderate risk for complex diseases will probably require much larger sample sizes than those needed for major gene diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the search for low/moderate cancer risk markers is still at its infancy, and that the data obtained from these studies should not be used for routine diagnostics.
the genetic basis of cancer is much more complex than previously thought.
the genetic basis of multifactorial disease is still far from being understood and that the identification of low/moderate risk genetic markers is not a straightforward process.
